title: Integration value loops battlecard - annotated wip
body:
Purpose:
This is a seller-facing battlecard and short playbook for targeting platform/integration teams that own embedding or app-level inference integrations. Focus: capture the recurring value loop (user -> model -> cached state -> app outcomes) and map it to Redwood levers (dedicated caching, routing policies, quantization profiles, private deployments). Not intended to be polished — a living working doc for SEs and field enablement.

One-liner value pitch (for platform integrators):
- Redwood reduces per-active-user inference cost while improving 99th-percentile latency through workload-aware caching and route-fallbacks, so your integration increases engagement without blowing up infra spend or violating data residency.

Buyer personas targeted:
- Platform Integrator (Technical) — cares about integration complexity, SDKs, infra footprint, and predictable unit economics.
- Product Lead (PM) — cares about feature velocity, retention lift, and measurable business metrics.
- Security/Compliance Owner — needs guarantees on data isolation, audit trails, and KMS/HSM compatibility.

Top objections and quick responses (seller-ready):
- "We can host models ourselves; why Redwood?"
  - Quick: Self-host often underestimates the ops cost: kernel selection, latency tail mitigation, and workload-aware batching. Redwood provides an operational runtime that adapts kernels and batching policies to your traffic mix — reducing token cost by up to single-digit percentages in typical chat/embedding workloads and preventing costly latency regressions during spikes.
- "Latency-critical — we can't tolerate cold starts."
  - Quick: Dedicated pools + warm-KV caching and targeted autoscale policies keep cold starts low. Bring up SLA window and fallback routing examples (see appendix).
- "We need on-prem for compliance."
  - Quick: Private deployment options (VPC + on-prem package) and KMS integrations are supported; include audit log examples and customer checklist.

Value loop mapping (high level):
1) Event: user action -> inference request
2) App layer: prefix caching / embeddings cache hit?
3) Model: selected variant (quantized / full precision) via routing policy
4) Runtime: batching + kernel selection -> response
5) Outcome: product metric update (click, retention, revenue)
6) Economic feedback: higher hit rates or cheaper model variants lower marginal cost leading to easier product experimentation (more iterations).

How to use this battlecard in a 12-minute SE call:
- 0:00–02:00 — 30s intro, 90s pain discovery (cost spikes, latency incidents, compliance).
- 02:00–05:00 — Value loop walk-through: show a simplified diagram (talk through caching -> routing -> fallbacks).
- 05:00–08:00 — Quick numbers: run a back-of-envelope for them (use the script below).
- 08:00–11:00 — Pilot proposal: scope (10k daily users, one endpoint), success metrics, timeline.
- 11:00–12:00 — Next steps: SE/Engineer technical deep-dive + legal intro if needed.

Back-of-envelope pilot math (script for the seller):
- Input from prospect: average request length 60 tokens, 2 requests per active user per day, peak concurrency 150 RPS, retention lift target +3% monthly.
- Redwood recommended pilot config: small dedicated pool (4x A100-equivalent), prefix cache enabled, model variant q4_0 for embeddings, fallthrough to fp16 variant for rare cases.
- Rough cost calc (seller-facing):
  - Token units per day = 60 * 2 * 10,000 = 1,200,000 tokens/day
  - Cache hit assumption = 40% -> effective token billable = 720k tokens/day
  - Using host-tier price proxy (internal guide) => ballpark $X/day (replace during call with current rates).
  - Expected latency improvement: median -30%, p99 -25% (based on analogous pilots).
- Seller tip: frame economics in terms of cost-per-retained-user rather than raw $/token.

Pilot success criteria (example):
- Latency: p95 < 350ms for typical conversation flows.
- Cost: pilot burn <= 120% of committed credit estimate.
- Product lift: measurable +2–4% retention over 30 days for pilot cohort.
- Ops: no PII exfiltration events; audit logs present.

Technical appendix (quick bullets to hand to an engineer in the call):
- SDKs and telemetry: Node/Python SDK with request tags for routing policy and warm-up hooks.
- Observability: per-token costs, token-level breakdowns by route, tracing hooks exposed via our console.
- Fallbacks: canary -> heterogenous model fallback (q4 -> fp16 -> fallback-hosted small model).
- Deployment: private with KMS + HSM; can ship an air-gapped image for on-prem ops.

Seller scripts and short quips (snappy):
- "Think of caching like reducing 'reader friction' — more hits means more cheap answers and room to experiment."
- "Our job is to make your unit economics predictable so your PMs can run fast without surprise bills."

Competitive differentiation to call out quickly:
- Unified interface across hosted/dedicated/private — same API + same rollout controls (no rework when moving from pilot to enterprise).
- Smart routing that preserves SLAs: low-latency routing prioritized during spikes with automatic economics-aware fallbacks.
- Built-in quality monitoring + eval tie-ins so model changes don't silently regress product metrics.

Field play checklist (short):
- Pre-call: collect average request size, peak concurrency, top 3 latency pain points, security constraints.
- On-call: run value loop mapping, run pilot B/OE script, propose 6-week pilot with milestones.
- Post-call: upload notes to JIRA ticket, create Confluence pilot page template, schedule technical deep-dive.

Open questions to resolve (working list):
- Need updated internal pricing proxy for hosting vs dedicated to share realistic numbers (action: finance contact Evan Brooks).
- Verify example p99 improvements with infra team (SRE) for q4->fp16 transitions.
- Draft a short legal appendix for on-prem pilots (privacy & audit commitments).

Notes to self / TODOs: 
- Create one-pager visual (value loop diagram) for slide insert.
- Convert the B/OE script into a small spreadsheet template for sellers.
- A/B test two opening lines: economics-first vs latency-first — collect results from next 10 calls.
